mainTopic: When a seller may testify for his buyer: liens on movables, sales without a guarantee (רב פפא and רב זביד), and שמואל's rule about a sold field.
overview: The גמרא explains why someone who sold a cow or cloak can still testify for the buyer, even though the seller owes money. Movables (מטלטלי) are not liened to a creditor once they are sold, and even an אפותיקי does not follow an ox or donkey to a buyer. רבא explains that a slave is different because his designation becomes public. The גמרא then worries that the movables may have been liened together with land. It answers that the seller bought the item and sold it right away, and then that he never owned land at all, which also blocks a proof about a 'דאקני' lien. Next it challenges from רב פפא: if the item was never the seller's, the buyer can claim his money back. It answers that the buyer admits the animal came from the seller's donkey. It also brings רב זביד, who holds that a sale without a guarantee frees the seller from every claim. Finally the גמרא returns to שמואל's rule that a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, and begins to ask what case שמואל means.

steps.title: The case is an ordinary sale where movables are not liened
steps.stepSummary: The seller can testify because in an ordinary case the cow or cloak is not liened to his creditor, since movable property is never liened to a בעל חוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are dealing with a plain case, where the item is not liened to the creditor. Why not? Because they are movables, and movables are not liened to a creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the seller has no personal interest in the cow or cloak he sold: his creditor could never take it from the buyer anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the creditor could take the item from the buyer, the seller would want the buyer to keep it so his debt stays covered, and that would disqualify his testimony. But a creditor's lien only covers land (מקרקעי), not מטלטלי. So once the item is sold, the creditor has no claim on it, and the seller gains nothing by testifying.

keyTerms.meaning: In a plain case, with no special arrangement
Is liened (held as security for a debt)

phrases.english: In a plain case, where it is not liened to him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the seller's creditor. The cow or cloak is not held as security for his loan.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
They are movable property,
and movable property is not liened to a creditor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer from earlier on the daf about why the seller may testify about a cow or cloak.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the case to a plain sale and gives the rule that movables are not liened.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller has no stake, because his creditor cannot collect movables from a buyer.

steps.title: Even a 'cloak on his shoulders' clause does not reach sold items
steps.stepSummary: Even if the debtor wrote that the creditor may collect from his very cloak, that only works while the items are still in the debtor's hands, not after they were sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though he wrote to him that he may collect even from the cloak on his shoulders, that only applies while the items are still with the debtor. Once they are no longer with him, it does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a possible objection: what if the loan document explicitly covered the debtor's movables?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A clause like 'even from the cloak on my shoulders' lets the creditor collect from movables the debtor still owns. It does not create a lien that follows the item into a buyer's hands. So a sold cow or cloak is still safe from the creditor.

keyTerms.meaning: Still intact and in the debtor's possession

phrases.english: And even though he wrote to him
that he may collect even from the cloak on his shoulders,
that applies only when the items are still as they were,
phrases.notes: Literally 'in their own form.' He means the items are still with the debtor.

phrases.english: but when they are not as they were, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּכְתַב לֵיהּ מִגְּלִימָא דְּעַל כַּתְפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a possible objection to step 1 before anyone raises it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A written clause covering movables lets the creditor collect only from movables still in the debtor's possession, not from sold ones.

steps.title: Even a designated אפותיקי cannot be taken from the buyer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes further: even if the cow or cloak had been made an אפותיקי, the creditor still cannot take it from the buyer. The reason comes from רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, even if he made it an אפותיקי, the creditor still cannot collect it. Why? Because of what רבא said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא widens its claim to the strongest case, an item formally designated for the debt. It then sets up רבא's statement as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אפותיקי is an item set aside specifically for a creditor, which normally gives him the strongest possible claim. The גמרא says that even this does not let him take an animal or cloak from a buyer. The word 'אלא' signals that we don't even need the plain-case limit from step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: An item specifically designated as the source for paying a debt

phrases.english: Rather, even if he made it an apoteiki,
phrases.notes: An apoteiki is property set aside as the payment source for a loan. Here 'it' is the cow or cloak.

phrases.english: the creditor also cannot collect it.
What is the reason? It follows Rava.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ עֲשָׂאוֹ אַפּוֹתֵיקֵי נָמֵי לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the plain-case limit of step 1 with a broader claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even an animal or cloak designated as an אפותיקי cannot be collected from a buyer.

steps.title: רבא: a slave versus an ox or donkey as אפותיקי
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a creditor can collect a slave that was made an אפותיקי and then sold, but cannot collect a sold ox or donkey that was made an אפותיקי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: if someone made his slave an אפותיקי and then sold him, the creditor collects from him. If he made his ox or donkey an אפותיקי and sold it, the creditor does not collect from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבא's ruling to support step 3: animals designated as an אפותיקי are not collected from a buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא draws a line between two kinds of movables. A slave designated as an אפותיקי stays liened even after a sale. An ox or donkey does not. A cow or cloak falls on the ox-and-donkey side, so the buyer keeps it.

phrases.english: As Rava said:
If he made his slave an apoteiki and then sold him,
the creditor collects from him.
If he made his ox or donkey an apoteiki and then sold it,
the creditor does not collect from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רָבָא: עָשָׂה עַבְדּוֹ אַפּוֹתֵיקֵי וּמְכָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source promised by 'כדרבא' in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That a cow or cloak made an אפותיקי cannot be taken from a buyer.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's ruling that an ox or donkey made an אפותיקי and then sold is not collected.

steps.title: The reason: a slave's designation becomes public
steps.stepSummary: The difference is publicity: designating a slave as an אפותיקי becomes known, while designating an animal does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? This one has publicity, and that one has no publicity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבא treats a slave differently from an ox or donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a slave is designated, people find out, so the buyer knew what he was getting into and the creditor can take the slave. Designating an animal is not publicized, so the buyer bought in good faith and the creditor cannot take it from him. A cow or cloak is like the animal, so the seller has no stake and may testify.
steps.whatToRemember: Movables cannot be collected from a buyer, even if they were made an אפותיקי, unless the designation is public, as with a slave. So the seller of a cow or cloak gains nothing from his testimony.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
This one has publicity,
and that one has no publicity.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the ox or donkey.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הַאי אִית לֵיהּ קָלָא, וְהָא לֵית לֵיהּ קָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind רבא's distinction in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lien that is publicized follows the item to a buyer; a lien that is not publicized does not.

steps.title: Challenge: maybe the movables were liened together with land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא worries that the debtor may have liened his movables to the creditor together with land. רבה rules that such a lien works, and רב חסדא adds that it requires a clause saying the document is binding and not just a formula.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that maybe he transferred the movables to him together with land! For רבה said: if he transferred movables together with land, the creditor acquires the land and acquires the movables. And רב חסדא said: that is only when he wrote, 'not as an אסמכתא and not as a standard template of documents.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the conclusion that the seller has no stake. Maybe the cow or cloak really was liened through land, so the creditor could take it after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Movables can be liened 'together with' land (אגב מקרקעי), and רבה says such a lien works for both. רב חסדא adds that the document must say it is not an אסמכתא and not a mere template, so that it is clearly binding. If that happened here, the seller would gain from his testimony, and the earlier answer would break down.

keyTerms.meaning: A commitment made without full intent, which does not bind
A standard template of documents, written but not meant seriously

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'אקני מטלטלי אגב מקרקעי' does not mean the creditor owns the movables now. It means they are liened to him through the land, so he could collect them later.

phrases.english: But let us be concerned that perhaps
he transferred movable property to him by means of land!
phrases.notes: 'He' is the seller-debtor and 'him' is his creditor.

phrases.english: As Rabba said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַקְנִי לֵיהּ מִטַּלְטְלֵי אַגַּב מְקַרְקְעֵי –
phrases.english: If he transferred movable property to him by means of land,
he acquires the land and acquires the movable property.
And Rav Ḥisda said:
And that is only where he wrote to him:
"Not like an asmakhta
and not like a template of documents."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא אַקְנִי לֵיהּ מִטַּלְטְלֵי אַגַּב מְקַרְקְעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion that the creditor can never take the cow or cloak from the buyer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the seller has no stake because the movables are not liened to his creditor.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Movables liened together with land are liened to the creditor, as רבה and רב חסדא rule. So the creditor might take them from the buyer, which gives the seller a stake in his testimony.

steps.title: The seller bought the item and sold it right away
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the seller bought the movable item and sold it immediately, so no creditor's lien could have attached to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? One where he bought the item and sold it right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry from step 6, that the movables might have been liened to a creditor together with land. It does this by limiting the case to an item the seller bought and immediately sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lien can only attach while an item is in the debtor's hands. If he bought it and sold it at once, there was no time for a creditor's lien to take hold. So the seller has no debt-related reason to want the item to stay with the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? This is a standard way to narrow a ruling to a specific case.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
For example, where he bought it and sold it immediately.
phrases.notes: He means the seller had the item for only a moment, too short for any creditor's lien to grab it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry in step 6 that the movables were liened together with land.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The movables might have been liened to a creditor together with land, which would give the seller an interest.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller bought and resold the item at once, so no lien ever attached to it.

steps.title: Worry about a lien on property bought later
steps.stepSummary: Even if the item was bought and sold immediately, the debtor may have written that future purchases are also liened to the creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that perhaps he wrote 'what I will acquire' is also liened!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 7. A debtor can lien even property he buys in the future, so buying and selling quickly may not stop the lien.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the loan document said 'דאקני' (what I will acquire), the lien could attach the moment the seller bought the item. In that case the speed of the resale would not help, and the seller would still have an interest.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That which I will acquire': a clause liening property the debtor buys in the future

phrases.english: But let us be concerned that perhaps it is a case of 'what I will acquire'!
phrases.notes: He means the loan document may have said: 'I will repay even from what I buy later.'

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the item was bought and immediately sold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A 'דאקני' clause would make the lien attach at the moment of purchase, so a quick resale does not prevent it.

steps.title: Does this prove a lien on later purchases fails once they are sold?
steps.stepSummary: Since the case ignores the 'דאקני' worry, the גמרא asks whether this shows that a lien on future purchases does not hold once the item is sold or inherited.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you learn from this that with 'what I will acquire,' if he bought and sold, or bought and left it to heirs, it is not liened?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the worry into a possible proof. If the ruling stands without worrying about 'דאקני,' maybe that kind of lien does not work against buyers or heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether 'דאקני' property that was bought and then sold or inherited is still liened is a known open question. The גמרא checks whether this case quietly settles it in favor of 'not liened.'

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: we can conclude from this
He bought and then left it to his heirs
Is liened, held as security for the debt

phrases.english: Do you learn from it: 'what I will acquire,'
if he bought and sold, or bought and bequeathed,
it is not liened?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the worry of step 8 into a proposed proof about the law of 'דאקני'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the ruling imply that 'דאקני' property bought and then sold or inherited is not liened?

steps.title: No proof: the seller never owned land
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The case is one where witnesses know the seller never owned land, so no lien on movables could exist at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where witnesses say: we know about this man that he never had land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 9 by setting up a different case. Here witnesses testify that the seller never owned any land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lien on movables only works together with land, as step 6 explained. If the seller never had land, his movables could not be liened, whether bought now or later. So the case says nothing about the open question of 'דאקני'.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed for that; it is needed for a different case

steps.whatToRemember: The ruling is set in a case where the seller never owned land, so no creditor could have a lien on his movables. That is why the case proves nothing about 'דאקני'.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary where witnesses say:
We know about this one
that he never had land.
phrases.notes: Without land, movables can't be liened, as step 6 explained, so there is no lien to worry about.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 9 and removes the worry of step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that a 'דאקני' lien fails once the item is sold or inherited.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed a lien was possible. In the actual case the seller never had land, so no lien on movables could exist.

steps.title: רב פפא: the buyer can go back to the seller if the item was never his
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges from רב פפא. Even without a guarantee, if the item turns out not to belong to the seller, the buyer can claim his money back, so the seller still has an interest.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב פפא said: even though חכמים said that if someone sells a field without a guarantee and a creditor takes it, the buyer cannot go back to the seller, if it turns out the field was not his, the buyer can go back to him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge from רב פפא's rule. If the claimant proves the item was never the seller's, the buyer can demand his money back from the seller.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 7-10 only removed the creditor-lien reason for the seller's interest. רב פפא shows another reason: the buyer can sue the seller if the item was never the seller's. So the seller still gains if the item stays with the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? This introduces a challenge from another ruling.
A guarantee: the seller's promise to repay if the buyer loses the property
He seized it from the buyer to collect his debt
He goes back to him, meaning he can claim his money back from the seller

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. A creditor taking the field is the seller's debt problem, which a sale without a guarantee does not cover. A field that was never the seller's is a broken sale, so the buyer can claim his money back even without a guarantee.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that removing the lien problem is not enough. The seller can still have a personal interest because of the buyer's claim against him.

phrases.english: But didn't רב פפא say:
even though the Sages said:
One who sells a field to his fellow without a guarantee,
and a creditor came and seized it,
the buyer cannot go back to the seller;
but if it is found that it was not his, he can go back to him!
phrases.notes: Apply this to our case: if the cow or cloak was never the seller's, the buyer will demand his money back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the main question of the seller's interest and challenges the cases set up in steps 7 and 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that, in these cases, the seller has nothing to gain if the item stays with the buyer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By רב פפא's rule, if the item is shown not to be the seller's, the buyer can claim his money back. So the seller still has a personal interest.

steps.title: The buyer admits the foal came from the seller's donkey
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the buyer recognizes the animal as the offspring of the seller's donkey, so he can never claim the seller had no right to sell it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the buyer recognizes that this animal is the offspring of the seller's donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from רב פפא by narrowing down the case. The buyer himself admits the animal was born to the seller's donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא said that if the item turns out not to belong to the seller, the buyer can get his money back. That would give the seller something to gain from his testimony. Here, however, the buyer admits the animal came from the seller's own donkey, so he cannot claim the seller sold him something that was not his. The seller therefore has nothing to gain, and he may testify.

keyTerms.meaning: "What case are we dealing with here?" The opening for narrowing a case to answer a challenge.

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
With a case where he recognizes it,
phrases.notes: The one who recognizes the animal is the buyer.

phrases.english: that it is the offspring of his donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רב פפא in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because of רב פפא, it seemed the seller always has a stake, since the buyer could claim his money back if the item is not the seller's.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the buyer admits the animal came from the seller's donkey, he can never make that claim, so the seller has no stake and may testify.

steps.title: רב זביד: without a guarantee, the buyer cannot come back at all
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד disagrees with רב פפא. Even if the item turns out not to be the seller's, the buyer cannot claim his money back, because that is exactly what selling without a guarantee means.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד says: even if it turns out the item was not the seller's, the buyer cannot come back to him. The seller can say to him: "This is exactly why I sold it to you without a guarantee."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב זביד, who disagrees with רב פפא. In his view, a seller who gave no guarantee owes the buyer nothing, even if the item was never his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא held that "no guarantee" covers only a creditor seizing the item. If the seller never owned it, the buyer still gets his money back. רב זביד holds that "no guarantee" covers everything, so a seller who gave no guarantee owes nothing even if the item was never his.

keyTerms.meaning: Without a guarantee. The seller does not promise to pay back the buyer if the item is taken away.
He cannot come back to him to claim his money.

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows two ways to understand a sale "without a guarantee": does it cover only a creditor seizing the item, or also a case where the seller never owned it?

phrases.english: But רב זביד says:
Even if it is found that it was not his,
phrases.notes: "His" means the seller's. רב פפא said the opposite in this very case.

phrases.english: he cannot come back to him,
since he can say to him:
This is why I sold it to you
without a guarantee.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a view opposing רב פפא, whose statement was the basis of the challenge in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sale without a guarantee frees the seller from all claims, even if the item turns out not to have been his.

steps.title: Back to שמואל: a seller cannot testify about the field he sold
steps.stepSummary: רבין בר שמואל, quoting שמואל, says that even someone who sold a field without a guarantee cannot testify for the buyer about it, because he is keeping it available for his own creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now let us look at the statement itself. רבין בר שמואל said in the name of שמואל: someone who sells a field to another person without a guarantee cannot testify for him about that field, because he is keeping it in place for his own creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the original statement of שמואל, which was quoted earlier, in order to look at it carefully. The rule is that the seller cannot testify, even when he gave no guarantee.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a seller without a guarantee has nothing to lose if the buyer loses the field. But the seller does have a stake. As long as the field stays with the buyer, the seller's creditor can collect his debt from it, and that pays off the seller's debt. So his testimony helps himself, and he cannot be a witness.

keyTerms.meaning: "The matter itself." The גמרא is going back to examine a statement quoted earlier.
He keeps the field in place for his own creditor to collect from.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think "no guarantee" means the seller has no stake at all. Even without a guarantee, the seller gains if the field stays where his own creditor can collect from it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base statement the whole discussion has been testing. Every step until now was about whether a seller's own interest disqualifies his testimony.

phrases.english: The matter itself:
phrases.notes: The גמרא now goes back to take a closer look at שמואל's statement that it quoted earlier.

phrases.english: רבין בר שמואל said
in the name of שמואל:
One who sells a field to his fellow
without a guarantee
cannot testify for him about it,
because he is keeping it in place
for his creditor.
phrases.notes: If the field stays with the buyer, the seller's creditor can take it to collect the seller's debt.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא אָמַר רָבִין בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion and goes back to examine the base statement of שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller, even without a guarantee, cannot testify for the buyer about the field he sold, because he has a stake in keeping it available for his creditor.

steps.title: What case is שמואל talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact situation in which שמואל's rule applies.
steps.whatsHappening: This short question sets up the next step. The גמרא wants to know exactly what case שמואל means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule depends on who is challenging the buyer and what the seller would be testifying about. The גמרא asks for the case so it can see exactly how the seller's creditor comes into the picture.

keyTerms.meaning: "What are the circumstances?" A request to spell out the exact case.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact case behind the rule of שמואל in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The specific situation in which the seller's testimony would keep the field available for his creditor.
